rw: Revenue is earned as service is performed: $4,000 / 4 months = $1,000 per month, so $1,000 is recognized now and $3,000 stays in Unearned Revenue.

ww.$3,000: This $3,000 figure is the revenue still unearned after one month, not the amount recognized; the remaining 3 of 4 months stay as a liability until performed.
ww.$4,000: This is the full prepayment of $4,000, but revenue cannot be recognized all at once when only 1 of the 4 months of service has been performed.
ww.$0: Zero would be right only if no service had been performed yet; here one month is complete, so $1,000 of the prepayment has been earned as revenue.

rw: Temporary accounts (revenue, expenses and drawings) are closed at period end so they start the next period at zero, and their balances move into capital.

ww.Asset accounts such as cash and land: Assets like cash and land are permanent (real) accounts; their balances carry forward to the next period and are never closed to zero at period end.
ww.Capital account balance, which carries o: The capital account is permanent: it receives the closing entries and carries its balance into the next period, so it is not itself closed.
ww.Liability accounts such as payables: Liabilities such as accounts payable are permanent balance sheet accounts; they keep their balances into the next period and are not closed.

rw: In closing, Income Summary is closed to the owner's Capital account, so $12,000 of net income increases Owner's Capital, which is permanent equity.

ww.Revenue sales: Revenue is a temporary account that is itself closed out at period end; it feeds net income but does not receive the net income transfer.
ww.Accounts Payable: Accounts Payable is a liability showing what the business owes suppliers; net income increases owner's equity, not a liability balance.
ww.Cash on hand: Cash is an asset that is not affected by the closing entries; profit is recorded in equity, not moved into the cash account.

rw: After closing entries, only permanent accounts (assets, liabilities, capital) have balances, so this trial balance confirms debits equal credits before the next period.

ww.A budget that managers use to plan spend: A budget is a forward-looking plan for spending, while a post-closing trial balance is a backward-looking check of ledger balances after closing.
ww.A list of expenses that the firm has pai: Listing expenses paid describes an expense report; a post-closing trial balance contains no expenses because those accounts were closed to zero.
ww.A trial balance before adjustments, prep: That describes an unadjusted trial balance, taken before adjusting entries; the post-closing version is prepared after closing and lists only permanent accounts.

rw: The unadjusted trial balance lists ledger balances before adjusting entries, proving debits equal credits and showing which accruals and deferrals still need adjustment.

ww.Never prepared by any accountant in the: Accountants routinely prepare an unadjusted trial balance as a check on the ledger before making adjusting entries, so it is a normal step.
ww.After adjusting entries are all posted t: A trial balance after adjusting entries is the adjusted trial balance, a later step; the unadjusted one comes before those entries are posted.
ww.After closing entries are all posted to: A trial balance taken after closing entries is the post-closing trial balance, which includes only permanent accounts; it is not the unadjusted version.

rw: The adjusted trial balance is prepared after adjusting entries are posted, and it is the source for preparing the financial statements.

ww.A trial balance prepared before the adju: A trial balance prepared before adjusting entries is the unadjusted trial balance, the earlier step; the adjusted version reflects accruals and deferrals.
ww.A budget that managers use to plan spend: A budget is a spending plan for the future; the adjusted trial balance is a list of account balances after adjustments, used to build statements.
ww.After closing entries are posted to the: A trial balance after closing entries is the post-closing trial balance, which has only permanent accounts; the adjusted trial balance comes before closing.

rw: Net income from the income statement goes to the statement of owner's equity, whose ending capital goes on the balance sheet, so this order is required.

ww.Any order that the accountant likes best: Statements must follow a set order because each feeds the next; letting the accountant choose freely would break the flow of net income into equity.
ww.Equity statement first, then the balance: Starting with the equity statement fails because it needs net income, which the income statement has not yet produced.
ww.Balance sheet first, then the income and: The balance sheet needs ending capital from the equity statement, which needs net income from the income statement, so the balance sheet comes last.

rw: A calendar year runs January 1 to December 31; businesses using it have a fiscal year that matches the calendar, which simplifies tax reporting.

ww.Any 12 months in a row: Any 12 months in a row can describe a fiscal year, which may start in any month; a calendar year has fixed start and end dates.
ww.July 1 to June 30 each year: July 1 to June 30 is a common fiscal year (used by many governments and schools), not a calendar year, which runs January through December.
ww.A quarter of the whole year: A quarter is only three months, one fourth of a year, so it cannot be the whole 12-month calendar year.

rw: Posting copies each journal debit to the matching ledger account on the debit side, so the ledger shows the running balance of every account.

ww.Creates a statement for the customer and: Mailing a statement to a customer is billing, not posting; posting is the internal step of moving journal amounts into the ledger accounts.
ww.Deletes the entry from the journal of th: Posting does not delete journal entries; the journal remains the permanent original record, and posting just copies amounts into the ledger.
ww.Pays the bill that the firm owes to its: Paying a supplier is a separate cash transaction; posting is a bookkeeping step that records amounts and does not itself move any money.

rw: A T account is a simplified ledger form shaped like a T, with debits on the left and credits on the right, used to see an account's activity.

ww.A tax account that is used to track a fi: A T account has nothing to do with taxes owed to the IRS; the T refers to the shape of the form used to show debits and credits.
ww.A time record that shows the hours each: Hours worked by employees are tracked on timesheets or time cards, not in a T account, which records debits and credits for one account.
ww.A trial form that lists every account ba: A list of every account balance is a trial balance; a T account shows only one account, and the T is the form's shape.

rw: Cash is an asset with a normal debit balance: $9,000 debits - $6,500 credits = $2,500, which is a debit balance.

ww.$0 balance: A zero balance would require debits equal to credits; here debits of $9,000 exceed credits of $6,500, so the account has a balance left over.
ww.$15,500 debit: This adds the debits and credits together ($9,000 + $6,500); a T account balance is the difference between the two sides, not the sum.
ww.$2,500 credit: The $2,500 amount is right, but debits are larger than credits, so the balance falls on the debit side and cannot be a credit.

rw: Accounts Payable is a liability with a normal credit balance: $7,500 credits - $3,000 debits = $4,500 credit, still owed to suppliers.

ww.$0 balance: A zero balance would need debits equal to credits; here the two sides differ ($3,000 versus $7,500), so a balance remains.
ww.$4,500 debit: The amount is correct, but credits ($7,500) exceed debits ($3,000), so the balance sits on the credit side and cannot be a debit.
ww.$10,500 credit: This adds the two sides ($3,000 + $7,500); the balance is the difference between debits and credits, which is $4,500, not the sum.

rw: A sale on account means the customer has not paid yet, so Accounts Receivable is debited for the $1,500 owed and Sales revenue is credited.

ww.Debit Cash and credit the Receivable: Debiting Cash is wrong because no cash was received in an on-account sale, and crediting the Receivable would reduce what customers owe.
ww.Debit Payable and credit the Sales: Accounts Payable is a liability for money the business owes others; a sale creates a receivable, an asset, so debiting Payable is wrong.
ww.Debit Sales and credit Receivable for it: Debiting Sales and crediting Receivable reverses the sale (it would be a return or cancelled sale), rather than recording a new sale of $1,500.

rw: Cash increases (debit) and Accounts Receivable decreases (credit) by $1,500; one asset is swapped for another, so total assets and revenue are unchanged.

ww.Debit Cash and credit Sales Revenue: Crediting Sales Revenue would count the sale a second time; revenue was recorded when the sale was made, and this payment only collects the receivable.
ww.Debit Sales and credit Cash received: Debiting Sales would reduce revenue; collecting a customer's payment does not change revenue, only the form of the asset from receivable to cash.
ww.Debit Receivable and credit Cash in full: This is reversed: debiting Receivable would increase what customers owe, while a collection should decrease the Receivable with a credit.

rw: Inventory (an asset) increases with a debit, and Accounts Payable (a liability) increases with a credit of $800 because the business owes the supplier.

ww.Debit Merchandise Inventory, credit Cash: Crediting Cash would be right for a cash purchase, but the question says on account, so no cash leaves the business yet.
ww.Debit Payable, credit Inventory, as if p: This is reversed and treats the purchase as paid: it would reduce inventory and payable, but buying on account raises both inventory and the payable.
ww.Debit Cash, credit Merchandise Inventory: Debiting Cash would increase cash, which is the opposite of a purchase; buying inventory raises inventory with a debit and does not bring in cash.

rw: Paying the supplier decreases the liability, so Accounts Payable is debited $800, and Cash is credited because the asset decreases by the same amount.

ww.Debit Inventory, credit Receivable: Debiting Inventory is wrong because paying a bill does not buy goods, and a Receivable is money owed to the business, not by it.
ww.Debit Cash and credit the Payable: Crediting the Payable would increase what is owed; paying a supplier should reduce the liability with a debit and reduce Cash with a credit.
ww.Debit Expense and credit the Cash: Debiting an Expense would record a new cost; the expense or inventory was recorded when purchased, so payment only settles the existing payable.

rw: 2/10, n/30 means a 2% discount if paid within 10 days; otherwise the full (net) amount is due within 30 days of the invoice date.

ww.A 10% discount if paid in 2 days, with n: The terms are 2/10, so the discount is 2%, not 10%, and the 10 refers to the discount period, not the due date; the net is due in 30 days.
ww.2 days discount within 10 months, with a: This misreads days as months; credit terms use days, so 10 and 30 refer to days after the invoice date, not months.
ww.Net amount due in full after 2 days from: The net amount is due in 30 days, not 2 days; the 2 in the terms is the discount percentage, which applies if paid within 10 days.

rw: Day 8 is within the 10-day discount period, so the discount is 2% x $2,000 = $40, and the amount due is $2,000 - $40 = $1,960.

ww.$2,040: This adds the discount ($2,000 + $40) instead of subtracting it; paying early earns a discount, so the payment is lower than the invoice.
ww.$1,800: This subtracts a 10% discount ($200); the terms give 2% (the 10 is the number of days), so the discount is $40, not $200.
ww.$2,000: Paying the full $2,000 would be due only after the discount period ends (day 11 to 30); on day 8 the 2% discount is available.

rw: Day 10 is the last day of the discount period, so the discount is 3% x $5,000 = $150, and the payment would be $4,850.

ww.$500: This is 10% of $5,000 ($500); the discount rate is 3%, and the 10 in the terms is the number of days to qualify for it.
ww.$15: This is 0.3% of $5,000 ($15), a misplaced decimal; the 3% rate gives $5,000 x 0.03 = $150.
ww.$1,500: This is 30% of $5,000; the 30 in the terms is the due date in days, not the discount percentage, which is 3%.

rw: The buyer issues a debit memo to reduce the amount owed to the seller, such as for returned or damaged goods, which debits Accounts Payable.

ww.A receipt for payment that a seller give: A receipt for payment is given to a buyer after a cash sale; it is not a debit memo, which adjusts an amount owed on account.
ww.A check written by a firm to pay a suppl: A check written to pay a supplier is a payment (a cash disbursement); a debit memo is a document that reduces a payable rather than paying it.
ww.A bill increasing amounts owed, which a: A bill increasing what the buyer owes is an invoice or a credit memo from the seller's view; a debit memo reduces what the buyer owes.

rw: The allowance method estimates uncollectible accounts and records bad debt expense in the same period as the sales, which matches expenses to revenues.

ww.Writing off a debt only when a customer: That is the direct write-off method, which expenses a debt only when it proves uncollectible; the allowance method estimates the loss in advance instead.
ww.Charging customers more to cover the deb: Raising prices is a pricing decision and is not an accounting method for recording bad debts; the allowance method estimates and records the expected loss.
ww.Ignoring bad debts and leaving them out: Ignoring bad debts would overstate receivables and income; GAAP requires recognizing the expected loss, which the allowance method does by estimate.

rw: Under direct write-off, bad debt expense is recorded only when a specific account is deemed uncollectible, which can fall in a later period than the sale.

ww.Ignoring bad debts and leaving them out: Ignoring bad debts is not an accepted method; the direct write-off method does record the loss, but only once an account is actually written off.
ww.Charging customers more to cover the deb: Charging customers more is a pricing decision, not an accounting method; direct write-off records an expense when a specific account proves uncollectible.
ww.Estimating in advance the amount of debt: Estimating in advance describes the allowance method; the direct write-off method waits until an account is actually deemed uncollectible.

rw: Bad debt expense is the estimated percentage of credit sales: $200,000 x 1.5% = $3,000.

ww.$30,000: This uses 15% ($200,000 x 0.15 = $30,000); the rate is 1.5%, so the decimal is 0.015, not 0.15.
ww.$300: This uses 0.15% ($200,000 x 0.0015 = $300); 1.5% is 0.015 as a decimal, which gives $3,000.
ww.$1,500: This is half the correct amount, as if the rate were 0.75%; the 1.5% rate applied to $200,000 gives $3,000.

rw: The adjusting entry debits Bad Debt Expense (recognizing the loss) and credits Allowance for Doubtful Accounts, a contra-asset reducing receivables.

ww.Debit Receivable, credit Expense, for th: Debiting Receivable would increase what customers owe; the estimate of bad debts reduces receivables through an allowance, with the expense debited instead.
ww.Debit Cash and credit the Allowance for: Debiting Cash would imply cash was collected; recording the estimate involves no cash, only an expense debit and an allowance credit.
ww.Debit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts an: This is reversed: debiting the Allowance reduces it, as when writing off a specific account, and crediting Expense would lower expense instead of recording it.

rw: Net realizable value = gross receivables - allowance = $60,000 - $2,500 = $57,500, the amount the company expects to actually collect.

ww.$60,000: $60,000 is the gross accounts receivable; net realizable value is gross receivables less the allowance for doubtful accounts, so it must be lower.
ww.$62,500: This adds the allowance to receivables; the allowance is a contra-asset, which is subtracted, so net realizable value is $57,500.
ww.$2,500: $2,500 is just the allowance for doubtful accounts, the amount expected to be uncollectible, not the net amount expected to be collected.

rw: Receivables turnover = net credit sales / average accounts receivable, showing how many times a year the company collects its receivables.

ww.Cash divided by sales for the whole year: Cash divided by sales does not measure collection of credit sales; receivables turnover relates net credit sales to the average accounts receivable.
ww.Sales divided by inventory held at the e: Sales divided by inventory is related to inventory turnover, which measures how fast stock sells, not how fast receivables are collected.
ww.Assets divided by liabilities, to show i: Assets divided by liabilities is a solvency measure of whether debts can be met; it has nothing to do with collecting receivables.

rw: Receivables turnover = net credit sales / average receivables = $600,000 / $100,000 = 6 times, meaning receivables are collected about six times a year.

ww.$500,000: $500,000 is the difference between the sales and receivables ($600,000 - $100,000); a turnover ratio is a division, not a subtraction.
ww.60 times: This shifts the decimal; $600,000 / $100,000 = 6, not 60, so receivables turn over 6 times a year.
ww.0.17 times: This inverts the ratio ($100,000 / $600,000 = 0.17); turnover divides sales by receivables, giving $600,000 / $100,000 = 6 times.

rw: Average collection period = 365 / turnover = 365 / 6 = about 60.8, or roughly 61 days, the average time to collect a credit sale.

ww.About 2,190 days: This multiplies instead of dividing (365 x 6 = 2,190); the collection period is 365 divided by turnover, which gives about 61 days.
ww.About 365 days: 365 days is the whole year; dividing it by a turnover of 6 gives about 61 days, so the collection period is much shorter than a year.
ww.About 6 days: This is just the turnover figure restated as days; the collection period divides 365 by 6, giving about 61 days.

rw: A control account in the general ledger summarizes a subsidiary ledger, such as Accounts Receivable summarizing each customer's individual account balance.

ww.An account for tax that the firm pays to: An account for state tax payments is not a control account; a control account is a general ledger account that summarizes a subsidiary ledger.
ww.An account for budgets that the managers: A budget account is not a control account; control accounts like Accounts Receivable are summaries whose balance equals the total of the subsidiary ledger.
ww.An account for cash held by the firm in: Cash held in a bank or till is just a cash account; a control account must summarize the detail in a subsidiary ledger.

rw: A promissory note is a written promise by the maker to pay a specified sum on a specified date, and it may bear interest.

ww.A check written to a supplier by a firm: A check is an order to a bank to pay money; a promissory note is the maker's own written promise to pay and is not a check.
ww.A purchase order sent to a supplier to a: A purchase order is a buyer's request to a supplier for goods, not a promise to pay money on a set date.
ww.A receipt for cash paid that a seller ha: A receipt acknowledges cash already paid, whereas a promissory note is a promise to pay in the future.

rw: Interest = principal x rate x time = $5,000 x 0.06 x 3/12 = $75, because 3 months is one quarter of a year.

ww.$25: $25 would be the interest for one month at 6% on a smaller base or for one month at 1%; 3 months at 6% on $5,000 is $75.
ww.$300: This is a full year of interest at 6% ($5,000 x 0.06 = $300); the note runs only 3 months, which is 1/4 of a year, so $75.
ww.$900: This is 18% of $5,000 (6% for 3 full years); the rate is annual and the time is only 3 months, so $75.

rw: Dishonoring a note means the maker fails to pay at maturity; the holder then usually transfers the note and interest to Accounts Receivable.

ww.Selling the note to a bank before it mat: Selling a note to a bank before it matures is called discounting a note receivable, not dishonoring it.
ww.Renewing the note for a further period o: Renewing a note for a further period extends its term by agreement; it is not a default, so it is not dishonoring.
ww.Paying early, before the note falls due: Paying early is not a default; dishonor happens only when the maker fails to pay at maturity.

rw: Working capital = current assets - current liabilities = $30,000; it shows the liquid funds available to meet short-term obligations (a 1.5 current ratio supports it).

ww.$60,000: This is likely one of the component balances (such as current liabilities) rather than the difference between current assets and current liabilities, which is working capital.
ww.$150,000: This figure is not the difference between current assets and current liabilities; working capital subtracts liabilities from assets rather than adding or scaling them.
ww.1.5: A value of 1.5 is a ratio, which fits the current ratio (current assets / current liabilities), not working capital, which is stated in dollars.

rw: The quick (acid-test) ratio = quick assets (cash, marketable securities, receivables) divided by current liabilities, excluding inventory because it is harder to convert to cash.

ww.Net income over owner equity for the yea: Net income over owner equity is return on equity, a profitability ratio, not the quick ratio, which measures short-term liquidity.
ww.Sales over assets owned at the end of th: Sales over assets is asset turnover, an efficiency measure; the quick ratio compares liquid assets to current liabilities.
ww.All assets over liabilities including st: All assets over liabilities including stock is a broad solvency measure; the quick ratio uses only liquid assets and excludes inventory.

rw: Quick assets = cash + receivables = $10,000 + $20,000 = $30,000; divided by current liabilities of $30,000 gives 1.0, excluding inventory.

ww.0.5: 0.5 would result from using only cash ($10,000 / $30,000 = 0.33) or a similar mistake; the quick assets here include both cash and receivables.
ww.2.0: 2.0 would need $60,000 of quick assets; counting inventory ($10,000 + $20,000 + $30,000 = $60,000) is wrong because inventory is excluded.
ww.3.0: 3.0 would require $90,000 of quick assets; the quick ratio excludes inventory and uses only cash and receivables, so it cannot be this high.

rw: The debt ratio = total liabilities / total assets, showing the proportion of assets financed by creditors; a higher ratio means greater financial risk.

ww.Equity divided by total assets of the fi: Equity divided by total assets is the equity ratio; the debt ratio uses liabilities, and the two add up to 100% of assets.
ww.Assets divided by liabilities, as on the: Assets divided by liabilities flips the ratio; the debt ratio divides total liabilities by total assets to show the share of assets financed by debt.
ww.Net income divided by debt owed by the f: Net income divided by debt is not the standard debt ratio; it would mix a profit measure with a balance sheet item.

rw: Gross profit margin = gross profit / net sales, showing the percent of each sales dollar left after cost of goods sold.

ww.Sales divided by total assets owned: Sales divided by total assets is asset turnover, an efficiency ratio; gross profit margin measures profit after cost of goods sold.
ww.Net income over sales for the year: Net income over sales is net profit margin, which also subtracts operating expenses, interest and taxes; gross margin stops at cost of goods sold.
ww.Profit divided by the owner equity: Profit divided by owner equity is return on equity, which measures return to the owners, not the share of sales left after production costs.

rw: Gross profit = $500,000 - $300,000 = $200,000, and $200,000 / $500,000 = 40%, the share of sales left after cost of goods sold.

ww.200%: 200% wrongly treats the $200,000 gross profit as a percent; margin divides gross profit by net sales ($200,000 / $500,000), which is 40%.
ww.60%: 60% is cost of goods sold as a share of sales ($300,000 / $500,000); gross margin is the remainder, 40%, after subtracting that cost.
ww.0.4%: 0.4% mistakes the decimal 0.4 for a percentage; $200,000 / $500,000 = 0.4, which must be multiplied by 100 to give 40%.

rw: Net profit margin = net income / net sales, showing how many cents of each sales dollar remain as profit after all expenses.

ww.Net income over owner equity: Net income over owner equity is return on equity, which measures return to owners; net profit margin compares net income to net sales.
ww.Sales over the total assets owned: Sales over total assets is asset turnover, an efficiency ratio, and does not show how much of each sales dollar becomes profit.
ww.Gross profit divided over sales: Gross profit over sales is the gross profit margin, which ignores operating expenses, interest and taxes that net profit margin includes.

rw: ROA = net income / average total assets, measuring how efficiently a company uses its assets to generate profit.

ww.Net income over owner equity at the year: Net income over owner equity is return on equity (ROE), which uses equity instead of total assets as the base.
ww.Sales over assets owned by the firm at y: Sales over assets is asset turnover, which measures sales generated per dollar of assets rather than profit generated.
ww.Assets over liabilities, a ratio of solv: Assets over liabilities is a solvency ratio showing coverage of debts; it does not measure profitability from assets.

rw: ROA = net income / average total assets = $24,000 / $240,000 = 0.10, or 10%, meaning each dollar of assets earned ten cents.

ww.1%: 1% mistakes the decimal; $24,000 / $240,000 = 0.10, which is 10%, not 1%, so the decimal point was misplaced.
ww.1,000%: 1,000% is far too large; dividing $24,000 by $240,000 gives 0.10, and a profit of one tenth of assets is 10%.
ww.25%: 25% would require average assets of $96,000 ($24,000 / 0.25); with $240,000 of assets, the return is lower.

rw: Asset turnover = net sales / average total assets, showing how efficiently the firm uses its assets to generate sales.

ww.Cash over total assets held by the firm: Cash over total assets is a liquidity-type ratio; asset turnover measures how many sales dollars each dollar of assets produces.
ww.Assets over sales made in the year by th: This inverts the ratio (assets over sales); asset turnover puts sales on top, so a higher number means assets are used more efficiently.
ww.Net income over assets, as a percent: Net income over assets is return on assets (ROA), a profitability ratio; asset turnover is based on sales, not net income.

rw: EPS = (net income - preferred dividends) / weighted average common shares outstanding, showing profit attributable to each common share.

ww.Assets per share, which is the total ass: Total assets divided by shares is not EPS; EPS measures profit per share, not the book value of assets per share.
ww.Price per share, which is the market pri: Market price per share is what a share sells for today; EPS measures the profit earned per share instead.
ww.Dividends per share, which is the cash p: Dividends per share is the cash paid to each holder; EPS is the earnings per share, which may be larger or smaller than dividends.

rw: EPS = net income / shares outstanding = $600,000 / 200,000 = $3.00 per share (assuming no preferred dividends).

ww.$0.33: $0.33 inverts the division ($200,000 / $600,000); EPS divides net income by shares, so $600,000 / 200,000 = $3.00.
ww.$30: $30 would result from moving the decimal point; $600,000 divided by 200,000 shares is $3, not $30.
ww.$120: $120 multiplies the numbers incorrectly; EPS divides net income by shares outstanding, which gives $3.00.

rw: Times interest earned = operating income (EBIT) / interest expense, showing how many times earnings cover interest payments to lenders.

ww.Sales over interest expense for the year: Sales over interest expense is not the standard formula; interest coverage uses operating income, since sales do not show the profit available to pay interest.
ww.Debt over equity at the end of the year: Debt over equity is the debt-to-equity ratio, a leverage measure, not a measure of how well earnings cover interest.
ww.Net income over sales, shown as a percen: Net income over sales is net profit margin; it measures profit per sales dollar, not interest coverage.

rw: Times interest earned = operating income / interest expense = $90,000 / $15,000 = 6 times, meaning earnings cover interest six times over.

ww.0.17 times: 0.17 inverts the fraction ($15,000 / $90,000); times interest earned puts operating income on top, giving $90,000 / $15,000 = 6.
ww.$75,000: $75,000 is the difference ($90,000 - $15,000); the ratio is a division, and the result is a number of times, not dollars.
ww.105 times: 105 adds the two figures in thousands ($90 + $15); the ratio divides operating income by interest expense and equals 6.

rw: Percent change = (new - old) / old = ($230,000 - $200,000) / $200,000 = 0.15, a 15% increase in sales.

ww.13% increase: 13% is a miscalculation; the change is $30,000 on a base of $200,000, which is 15%, not 13%.
ww.15% decrease: The sales rose from $200,000 to $230,000, so the change is an increase, not a decrease; a decrease would mean sales fell.
ww.30% increase: 30% uses the dollar change in thousands ($30) as the percent; percent change = $30,000 / $200,000 = 15%, not 30%.

rw: The statement of cash flows reports cash from operating, investing and financing activities, which together explain the change in cash.

ww.Revenue, expense and net profit: Revenue, expense and net profit are items on the income statement, not the three sections of the statement of cash flows.
ww.Debit, credit and balance totals: Debit, credit and balance are accounting terms used in the ledger, not the categories on the cash flow statement.
ww.Assets, liabilities and equity: Assets, liabilities and equity are the three parts of the balance sheet, not the sections of the statement of cash flows.

rw: Buying equipment is an investing cash flow because it is a purchase of a long-term asset, along with buying land or investments.

ww.Taking a loan: Taking a loan is a financing activity because it raises money from creditors, not an investing activity.
ww.Customer receipts: Customer receipts are an operating cash flow from selling goods or services, not an investing activity.
ww.Paying wages: Paying wages is an operating cash flow, because it is a normal expense of running the business, not investing.

rw: Issuing stock raises money from owners, which makes it a financing cash flow, along with borrowing and paying dividends or debt.

ww.Customer receipts: Customer receipts are an operating cash flow from daily sales, not a financing activity involving owners or lenders.
ww.Buying land: Buying land is an investing cash flow, since land is a long-term asset; financing involves debt and equity.
ww.Buying inventory: Buying inventory is an operating cash flow, since inventory is part of daily business, not a financing activity.

rw: Collecting cash from customers is an operating cash flow, since it comes from the normal sales activity of the business.

ww.Paying dividends to owners: Paying dividends is a financing cash flow because it returns money to owners; operating flows relate to day-to-day sales and expenses.
ww.Buying a building for investing: Buying a building is an investing cash flow since it purchases a long-term asset; it is not part of day-to-day operations.
ww.Selling stock to investors: Selling stock to investors raises capital from owners, which is a financing cash flow rather than an operating one.

rw: Ending retained earnings = beginning + net income - dividends = $50,000 + $20,000 - $8,000 = $62,000.

ww.$70,000: $70,000 adds net income but forgets to subtract the $8,000 of dividends, which reduce retained earnings.
ww.$78,000: $78,000 adds the dividends ($50,000 + $20,000 + $8,000) instead of subtracting them; dividends reduce retained earnings.
ww.$38,000: $38,000 subtracts net income and dividends ($50,000 - $20,000 - $8,000); net income increases retained earnings, so it must be added.

rw: An unqualified (clean) opinion says the statements fairly present the company's position in all material respects, the best result for a company.

ww.An adverse opinion on the firm: An adverse opinion says the statements are not fairly presented; it is the opposite of the clean opinion that says they are fair.
ww.A disclaimer of opinion given: A disclaimer means the auditor could not form an opinion, such as when access was limited; it does not say statements are fair.
ww.A qualified opinion on one item: A qualified opinion says the statements are fair except for one specific item or limitation, so it is not a fully clean opinion.

rw: An adverse opinion means the statements do not fairly present the company's financial position because of material misstatements, the most negative audit result.

ww.The auditor disagrees with the company o: Disagreeing on one item, with a note, describes a qualified opinion; an adverse opinion is broader and covers the statements as a whole.
ww.The statements are fair in all material: Statements that are fair in all material respects describe an unqualified (clean) opinion, which is the opposite of an adverse opinion.
ww.The audit was not done because the compa: An audit that cannot be done because of denied access leads to a disclaimer of opinion, not an adverse opinion.

rw: The FASB sets U.S. GAAP as a private nonprofit board, and the SEC recognizes and enforces its standards for public companies.

ww.The SEC alone, for all companies and ban: The SEC has legal authority over public company reporting but relies on the FASB to set the standards; it does not set GAAP alone.
ww.The IRS, which collects taxes in the Uni: The IRS administers tax law; tax rules differ from GAAP, which is set by the FASB for financial reporting.
ww.The Federal Reserve, which sets bank rat: The Federal Reserve is the central bank that sets monetary policy and bank rates; it does not write accounting standards.

rw: The SEC requires public companies to file regular reports, such as the audited annual 10-K and quarterly 10-Q, so investors can make informed decisions.

ww.Only marketing plans and sales forecasts: Marketing plans and sales forecasts are internal documents; the SEC requires public companies to disclose audited financial results to investors.
ww.Only tax returns for the owners of the f: Tax returns of the owners are filed with the IRS; the SEC focuses on disclosure of the company's financial information for investors.
ww.No reports of any kind to the public at: The SEC exists to require public disclosure for investors, so public companies must file reports, not avoid reporting.

rw: Form 10-K is the annual report with audited financial statements that public companies file with the SEC, including business and risk disclosures.

ww.A tax form that businesses file with the: A tax form filed with a state revenue agency is not Form 10-K, which is filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
ww.A quarterly report filed with the SEC by: A quarterly report filed with the SEC is Form 10-Q, not 10-K; the 10-K is filed once a year.
ww.A loan application made by a firm to a b: A loan application to a bank is a private credit document; Form 10-K is a public disclosure filed with the SEC.

rw: Form 10-Q is the quarterly report with unaudited financial statements that public companies file with the SEC for each of the first three quarters.

ww.A loan application made to a bank: A loan application to a bank is a private credit request; Form 10-Q is a public report filed with the SEC.
ww.An annual report filed with the SEC: An annual report with audited statements is Form 10-K, filed once a year; the 10-Q covers each of the first three quarters.
ww.A tax form that firms file each year: A tax form for a yearly return is filed with a tax agency; Form 10-Q is an SEC filing about a company's quarterly results.

rw: Passed in 2002 after Enron and WorldCom, SOX strengthened financial reporting, internal controls, auditor independence and executive accountability for public companies.

ww.A law that set up deposit insurance and: Deposit insurance and bank capital rules came from banking laws such as the FDIC legislation, not from Sarbanes-Oxley, which targets public company reporting.
ww.A law that raised federal income tax rat: SOX did not raise federal income tax rates on large corporations; it concerns financial reporting, audits and internal controls at public companies.
ww.A law that gave workers the right to bar: The right of workers to bargain collectively comes from labor law such as the National Labor Relations Act, not from Sarbanes-Oxley.

rw: The PCAOB, created by Sarbanes-Oxley, oversees audits of public companies, setting auditing standards and inspecting accounting firms that audit them.

ww.A tax agency that collects income taxes: The IRS collects income taxes; the PCAOB is a nonprofit board created by Sarbanes-Oxley to oversee auditors, not to collect taxes.
ww.A stock exchange where shares of firms a: A stock exchange, such as the NYSE, is where shares trade; the PCAOB does not trade shares and instead oversees auditors.
ww.A bank regulator that sets reserve rules: Bank reserve rules are set by the Federal Reserve; the PCAOB oversees auditors of public companies, not banks.

rw: Segregation of duties splits tasks like authorizing, recording and custody among different people so no single person can commit and hide fraud.

ww.Keeping offices in separate buildings so: Segregation of duties is about dividing tasks between people, not about where offices are located in a city.
ww.Segregating customers by region so that: Separating customers by region is a sales organization choice and is not the internal control of dividing transaction duties among employees.
ww.One person doing everything alone, from: One person doing everything is the opposite of segregation of duties and a major fraud risk because nobody checks the work.

rw: The fraud triangle says fraud occurs when a person has pressure (motive), opportunity (weak controls) and rationalization (justifying the act).

ww.Profit, loss and cash, as in a ledger bo: Profit, loss and cash are financial terms, not the three elements of the fraud triangle that explain why people commit fraud.
ww.Audit, tax and law, as in a firm's offic: Audit, tax and law are accounting and legal fields, not the fraud triangle, which describes the conditions behind fraud.
ww.Debit, credit and balance, the ledger te: Debit, credit and balance are bookkeeping terms; the fraud triangle instead looks at the motive, chance and justification of the fraudster.

rw: Embezzlement is theft of money or property by someone entrusted with it, such as an employee or officer, and it is a form of fraud.

ww.A tax strategy used to cut yearly bills: A tax strategy to cut bills can be legal tax planning; embezzlement is a crime of stealing funds that were entrusted to a person.
ww.A legal fee paid to a lawyer for advice: A legal fee paid to a lawyer is a normal business expense, not embezzlement, which is a crime.
ww.A loan made by a bank to a firm in need: A bank loan to a firm in need is a lawful financing arrangement; embezzlement is theft by someone trusted with the funds.

rw: Integrity under the AICPA code means being honest and straightforward, so CPAs deal truthfully with clients, employers and the public.

ww.Serving only some clients so the account: Serving only some clients to stay focused is a business choice and is not integrity, which concerns honesty and straightforward dealing.
ww.Maximizing fees by charging clients as m: Maximizing fees by overcharging is not integrity; the code requires honest dealing and putting public trust ahead of personal gain.
ww.Hiding errors from the clients and from: Hiding errors from clients or the public is dishonest and violates integrity, which requires being honest and straightforward.

rw: Objectivity means being impartial and free of conflicts of interest, so professional judgment is not compromised by bias or outside influence.

ww.Favoring clients who pay the largest fee: Favoring clients who pay the largest fees is bias; objectivity requires impartial judgment that is not swayed by payment.
ww.Following rumors heard from friends and: Following rumors is not objectivity; accountants must base conclusions on facts and evidence, not on gossip from friends.
ww.Ignoring facts that do not suit the clie: Ignoring facts that do not suit the client is the opposite of objectivity, which requires weighing all facts impartially.

rw: Independence means an auditor has no financial or personal ties to the client that would impair judgment, so the opinion is trusted by the public.

ww.The auditor owning shares of stock in th: An auditor owning shares in the client has a financial interest that impairs independence, so it breaks the rule rather than defining it.
ww.The auditor working alone, with no other: Working alone is about staffing, not independence, which concerns freedom from financial or personal ties to the client.
ww.The auditor working for the client as an: An auditor employed by the client is not independent because the client's pay and control could bias the audit.

rw: Taxable income = gross income - deductions = $70,000 - $14,000 = $56,000, the amount on which tax is calculated.

ww.$70,000: $70,000 is gross income before deductions; taxable income is what remains after subtracting deductions from gross income.
ww.$14,000: $14,000 is only the amount of deductions; taxable income is gross income minus deductions, not the deduction alone.
ww.$84,000: $84,000 adds the deductions to gross income ($70,000 + $14,000); deductions reduce taxable income, so they are subtracted.

rw: A deduction lowers taxable income, saving tax at your rate, while a credit reduces the tax owed dollar for dollar, so credits are generally more valuable.

ww.A credit reduces taxable income while a: This reverses the definitions; a deduction, not a credit, reduces taxable income, while a credit reduces the tax owed.
ww.They are the same thing and both cut the: A deduction and a credit are different; a $1,000 credit saves $1,000 of tax, while a $1,000 deduction saves only that amount times your tax rate.
ww.A deduction cuts tax owed dollar for dol: This is reversed; credits cut tax owed dollar for dollar, while deductions reduce the taxable income to which the rates are applied.

rw: The marginal tax rate is the rate on the next or last dollar of income, the bracket rate that applies to an additional dollar earned.

ww.The average rate on all income earned: The average rate on all income is the effective tax rate; the marginal rate applies only to the last (highest) dollars earned.
ww.The lowest rate on any income earned: The lowest rate on any income is the bottom bracket rate; the marginal rate is the rate on the last dollar, usually higher.
ww.The sales tax rate on goods you buy: A sales tax on purchases is a different tax; the marginal rate refers to income tax brackets.

rw: The effective tax rate = total tax divided by total income, the average share of income actually paid in tax.

ww.The lowest rate in the tax table: The lowest rate in the tax table is the bottom bracket rate; the effective rate is an overall average, usually above it.
ww.The top rate paid on the last dollar: The top rate paid on the last dollar is the marginal rate; the effective rate averages over all income.
ww.The sales tax rate on purchases: A sales tax rate on purchases applies to spending; the effective tax rate refers to income tax paid compared with income.

rw: Effective tax rate = total tax / total income = $9,000 / $60,000 = 0.15, or 15%.

ww.9%: 9% is a misreading of the $9,000 tax; the effective rate = $9,000 / $60,000 = 0.15, which is 15%.
ww.6.7%: 6.7% results from inverting the numbers incorrectly ($4,000 / $60,000); the correct calculation is $9,000 / $60,000 = 15%.
ww.150%: 150% mistakes the decimal; a rate above 100% would mean paying more tax than the income earned, and $9,000 / $60,000 is 15%.

rw: Payroll taxes are taxes on wages paid, including Social Security and Medicare (FICA), and are shared by employer and employee.

ww.A tax on gifts that are given from one p: A tax on gifts is a gift tax, separate from payroll tax, which is levied on wages paid to employees.
ww.A tax on property such as land and homes: A tax on land and homes is a property tax, not a payroll tax, which is based on wages paid.
ww.A tax on sales of goods at the till in s: A tax on sales of goods in shops is a sales tax, not a payroll tax, which is based on wages paid.

rw: FICA = 6.2% + 1.45% = 7.65% of $4,000 = $248 + $58 = $306 withheld for Social Security and Medicare.

ww.$248: $248 is only the Social Security part ($4,000 x 6.2%); Medicare must be added, so the total is higher.
ww.$3,694: $3,694 is the pay left after FICA ($4,000 - $306), not the amount withheld; FICA is the withholding itself.
ww.$58: $58 is only the Medicare part ($4,000 x 1.45%); Social Security of $248 must be added to get the total FICA.

rw: Form 1099-NEC reports nonemployee compensation, which means payments made to independent contractors of $600 or more.

ww.Reporting interest paid by banks to save: Interest paid by banks to savers is reported on Form 1099-INT, not the 1099-NEC.
ww.Reporting wages paid to employees at yea: Wages paid to employees are reported on Form W-2, not on the 1099-NEC, which is for contractors.
ww.Applying for a license to run a small bu: A business license application is filed with the state or city, not reported on the 1099-NEC.

rw: Form W-2 reports an employee's annual wages and the taxes withheld, which the employer gives to the employee and the government.

ww.Applying for credit at a bank or with a: Applying for credit uses a loan application; Form W-2 is a tax reporting form, not a credit form.
ww.Reporting payments made to contractors i: Payments to contractors are reported on Form 1099-NEC, not on the W-2, which is for employees.
ww.Reporting sales tax collected from the s: Sales tax collected is reported on sales tax returns to the state, not on the Form W-2.

rw: Employers withhold income and payroll taxes from employees' pay, while independent contractors receive a 1099 and pay their own taxes, including self-employment tax.

ww.There is no difference in how taxes are: There are major differences; employers withhold and pay payroll taxes for employees, while contractors handle their own taxes.
ww.Contractors have taxes withheld by the h: Contractors are not subject to withholding by the hirer like employees; they receive full payment and pay their own taxes.
ww.Employees pay no taxes on the wages they: Employees do pay taxes on their wages, with income and payroll taxes usually withheld from each paycheck.

rw: Self-employment tax is the Social Security and Medicare tax paid by self-employed people, who pay both the employer and employee halves (15.3%).

ww.An import tax that is charged on goods t: An import tax is a tariff on goods entering the country, not a tax on self-employed individuals.
ww.A sales tax that shoppers pay on goods w: A sales tax is paid by shoppers on purchases; self-employment tax is based on net earnings from self-employment.
ww.A property tax that owners pay on land a: A property tax is paid on land and buildings; self-employment tax is not related to property ownership.

rw: Straight-line depreciation = (cost - salvage value) / useful life, which spreads the depreciable amount evenly over each year of the asset's life.

ww.Salvage value divided by cost of asset: Salvage value divided by cost does not give yearly depreciation; it would give a ratio rather than an annual expense amount.
ww.Cost times the useful life of the asset: Cost times useful life would give a number far larger than the asset's cost; depreciation spreads cost over the life instead.
ww.Cost plus salvage value of the asset: Adding salvage value to cost would overstate the depreciable amount; salvage value is subtracted because it will be recovered at the end.

rw: ($30,000 - $3,000) / 9 years = $27,000 / 9 = $3,000 of depreciation per year.

ww.$3,333: $3,333 divides the full cost of $30,000 by 9 years and ignores salvage value; the depreciable amount is cost less salvage value.
ww.$30,000: $30,000 is the machine's full cost; annual depreciation spreads the depreciable amount over 9 years rather than expensing it all at once.
ww.$27,000: $27,000 is the total depreciable amount ($30,000 - $3,000), not annual; dividing by 9 years gives $3,000 per year.

rw: MACRS (Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System) is the U.S. tax depreciation system using set recovery periods and accelerated deductions.

ww.A payroll rule that tells employers how: Payroll withholding rules come from IRS withholding tables; MACRS covers depreciation of business assets for tax purposes.
ww.A sales tax rule that tells stores how t: Sales tax collection rules are set by states; MACRS is a federal income tax depreciation method.
ww.A banking rule that tells banks how much: Bank reserve requirements are set by the Federal Reserve; MACRS is a tax depreciation method for business property.

rw: A tax lien is the government's legal claim on a taxpayer's property to secure payment of unpaid taxes, and it can affect credit and sale of the property.

ww.A tax deduction that lowers taxable pay: A tax deduction lowers taxable income; a tax lien is a legal claim on property, not a deduction.
ww.A tax credit that cuts the tax bill owed: A tax credit cuts the tax bill; a tax lien is a legal claim placed on property when taxes are unpaid.
ww.A tax refund paid back to the taxpayer i: A tax refund is money returned to a taxpayer who overpaid; a lien is a claim against property for unpaid taxes.

rw: A use tax applies to goods bought out of state, where no sales tax was charged, for use in your own state, so the state does not lose the tax.

ww.A tax on property that is owned by peopl: A tax on property owned is a property tax; a use tax applies to goods bought out of state and used in the buyer's state.
ww.A tax on gifts that one person gives to: A tax on gifts is a gift tax; a use tax is on goods bought elsewhere and used in your state.
ww.A tax on income that workers and firms e: A tax on income is an income tax; a use tax is related to purchases, not earnings.

rw: An excise tax is placed on specific goods or activities such as fuel, tobacco, alcohol or airline tickets and is often included in the price.

ww.A tax on payroll paid by employers on wa: A tax on payroll is a payroll tax; an excise tax applies to specific goods and services.
ww.A tax on all income earned by workers an: A tax on all income is an income tax; an excise tax applies to specific products and not to all earnings.
ww.A tax on property such as land and homes: A tax on land and homes is a property tax; an excise tax targets specific goods or services.

rw: Accounting software records, processes and reports financial transactions, such as invoices and payroll, with programs like QuickBooks.

ww.Programs for music players, used to play: Music player programs are entertainment software; accounting software handles financial transactions and records.
ww.Programs for editing photos and drawing: Photo editing and poster design programs are graphics software; accounting software deals with financial records.
ww.Programs for games, built for play and f: Game programs are entertainment software; accounting software is a business tool for financial recordkeeping.

rw: ERP (enterprise resource planning) software links accounting, HR, supply chain and other functions in one system, so departments share the same data.

ww.A tax form that businesses use to report: A tax form is filed with the IRS; ERP is business software that integrates operations, not a tax form.
ww.A spreadsheet used only by accountants t: ERP is not a one-account spreadsheet; it is a large integrated system used by many departments.
ww.A hardware part inside a computer that s: A hardware part storing files is a hard drive; ERP is software, not a hardware component.

rw: Cloud accounting uses software and data stored on internet servers instead of local machines, allowing access from anywhere and automatic updates.

ww.Weather reports that show how many cloud: Weather clouds are not related to cloud accounting, which refers to internet-based software and storage.
ww.A calculator that adds numbers for an ac: A calculator is a local device; cloud accounting runs on internet servers and handles far more than addition.
ww.A paper file that stores records in a dr: A paper file in a drawer is a physical record; the cloud means digital storage on internet servers.

rw: Blockchain is a secure distributed ledger that records transactions permanently, so entries are hard to alter and can be verified by many parties.

ww.A calculator that totals a column of num: A calculator totals numbers; blockchain is a shared digital ledger of transactions, not a calculating device.
ww.A paper ledger that is kept in a locked: A paper ledger in a locked office is a traditional record; blockchain is a digital ledger shared across a network.
ww.A tax form that businesses fill out and: A tax form is filed with the IRS; blockchain is a technology for recording transactions, not a tax document.

rw: RPA uses software bots to perform repetitive, rule-based tasks, such as data entry and invoice matching, freeing accountants for higher-value work.

ww.A tax rule that sets the rates for firms: A tax rule sets rates; RPA is software that automates tasks, not a tax rule.
ww.A spreadsheet formula that adds up a col: A spreadsheet formula adds numbers within a sheet; RPA bots work across applications to perform whole tasks.
ww.Physical robots that work in offices and: RPA bots are software, not physical robots, so they do not move paper around offices.

rw: Cybersecurity means protecting systems, networks and data from unauthorized access and attacks, which is vital for firms handling financial records.

ww.Selling computers and other devices to c: Selling computers and devices is a retail business; cybersecurity is the practice of protecting systems and data.
ww.Writing code for websites and phone apps: Writing code for websites and apps is software development, not cybersecurity, which protects systems.
ww.Printing documents and reports on paper: Printing documents is an office task, not cybersecurity, which protects digital systems and data.

rw: SUM adds all the numbers in a range of cells, as in =SUM(A1:A10).

ww.MAX: MAX returns the largest value in a range; it does not total the cells.
ww.COUNT: COUNT returns how many cells contain numbers; it does not add their values.
ww.AVERAGE: AVERAGE adds the cells and then divides by how many there are; it returns the mean, not the total.

rw: MAX returns the largest value in a range of cells, as in =MAX(A1:A10).

ww.COUNT: COUNT tells how many cells contain numbers, not which value is the largest.
ww.SUM: SUM adds a range to a total; it does not find the largest value.
ww.MIN: MIN finds the smallest value in a range, the opposite of what is asked.

rw: COUNT returns the number of cells in a range that contain numbers, as in =COUNT(A1:A10).

ww.AVERAGE: AVERAGE returns the mean of the numbers in a range; it does not count how many cells contain numbers.
ww.SUM: SUM adds the numbers in a range; it does not count how many cells have numbers.
ww.MAX: MAX returns the largest value in a range; it does not count cells.

rw: An absolute reference with dollar signs ($A$1) stays fixed on the same cell when the formula is copied, which is useful for constants like a tax rate.

ww.Changes when copied to the next cell dow: Changing when copied is the behavior of a relative reference like A1, not an absolute reference with dollar signs.
ww.Hides the cell from view on the sheet: Hiding cells is done with formatting commands; absolute references only control how a formula's cell address behaves when copied.
ww.Deletes the cell and all the data in it: Deleting a cell is a separate editing action; an absolute reference only locks the cell address in a formula.

rw: A relative reference like A1 adjusts to the new location when copied, so copying down a row changes A1 to A2.

ww.Stays fixed when it is copied: Staying fixed when copied is the behavior of an absolute reference ($A$1), not a relative reference like A1.
ww.Deletes the cell and its data: Copying a formula does not delete a cell or its data; a relative reference simply shifts to the new position.
ww.Hides the cell from the view: Hiding a cell is a formatting action; a relative reference only changes its address when copied.

rw: A bookkeeper records daily financial transactions, such as sales, purchases, payments and receipts, and keeps the books accurate.

ww.Files lawsuits for the company in court: Filing lawsuits is done by attorneys, not by bookkeepers who handle financial records.
ww.Designs products for sale to customers: Designing products is the job of designers and engineers, not bookkeepers.
ww.Sets strategy for the next ten years: Setting long-term strategy is a job for executives, not bookkeepers, who record transactions.

rw: A financial analyst evaluates financial data, trends and statements to guide investment or business decisions, often with forecasts and reports.

ww.Prepares payroll only, and handles nothi: Payroll preparation is a narrow clerical task; a financial analyst evaluates data to guide investment and business decisions.
ww.Records every sale made in the shop duri: Recording daily sales is done by a bookkeeper or cashier; a financial analyst studies data and makes recommendations.
ww.Audits tax returns for the revenue agenc: Auditing tax returns is the work of tax agency auditors, not financial analysts, who advise on investments and strategy.

rw: A cost accountant analyzes production costs, budgets and variances to help management control expenses and set prices.

ww.Prepares personal taxes for people who v: Preparing personal taxes is the work of a tax preparer; cost accountants work on internal costs.
ww.Audits public firms for the stock market: Auditing public firms is done by external auditors; cost accountants work inside a company on costs.
ww.Sells software to firms that need new sy: Selling software is a sales role; cost accountants analyze production costs.

rw: A controller oversees a company's accounting operations, financial reporting, internal controls and budgeting, usually reporting to the CFO.

ww.Manages the warehouse and the stock of g: Managing the warehouse and stock is an operations or inventory manager's job, not a controller's.
ww.Leads the sales team and sets monthly ta: Leading the sales team is the sales manager's job; a controller oversees accounting.
ww.Runs marketing campaigns and plans ads f: Running marketing campaigns is the marketing manager's job; a controller oversees accounting.

rw: A CFO is a top executive who leads financial strategy, reporting, capital raising and risk management and advises the CEO.

ww.Records daily entries in the books of th: Recording daily entries is a bookkeeper's job; a CFO is a top executive who leads financial strategy.
ww.Handles customer service and complaints: Customer service is handled by service managers; a CFO leads the company's financial function.
ww.Runs production lines and plans factory: Running production lines is an operations job, not the CFO's.

rw: The Certified Management Accountant (CMA) credential focuses on internal management accounting, covering planning, budgeting, cost analysis and performance management.

ww.A tax license that allows people to prep: A tax license for preparing returns relates to credentials like the EA or CPA, not the CMA, which focuses on management accounting.
ww.A sales license that allows people to ru: Running a retail shop is a business license matter, not an accounting certification like the CMA.
ww.A banking license that allows firms to t: A banking license to take deposits is granted to banks by regulators; the CMA is a professional accounting credential.
